label: Data Encryption Key (DEK)
type: the key that actually encrypts data at rest. DEKs are themselves encrypted by an encryption-at-rest key (the KEK), are rotated automatically by default on a configurable schedule, and can be forcibly replaced by 'dropping' them via REST - which also decrypts and re-encrypts the affected data.
evidence: Couchbase Server uses the keys you create directly to encrypt Data Encryption Keys (DEKs) which in turn encrypt your data.
When you drop the DEKs for a bucket or type of data, Couchbase Server creates a new replacement DEK.
You choose how frequently Couchbase Server rotates DEKs and (if you enable it) the encryption keys themselves.
note: The bottom of the native encryption-at-rest key hierarchy, whose top (encryption:encryption-at-rest-key, encryption:master-password) was already promoted. Round 26 deliberately did NOT merge this hierarchy with the system-secrets hierarchy (secrets:master-key -> secrets:data-key -> secrets:system-secret), even though both are two-level key-wrapping schemes rooted in the same master password and both use round 26's `encryptsKeysFor` predicate. No page in the corpus states a relationship between them, the things protected are different (cluster data versus on-disk configuration secrets), and all five secrets: members sit at recurrence 1 so the promotion rule declines them anyway. Recorded in reconciliation.md as an open question for an SME rather than resolved by resemblance.
relates_to_competency_question: Which key encrypts data at rest, and what encrypts that key?
